la:noun:lingua.html:
lingua (ante-class. form dingua, like dagrima for lacrima, Mar. Victorin. p. 2457 and 2470 P.; cf. the letter D), ae, f.
Sanscr. jihvā; original Lat. form. dingua; A. -S. tunga; Germ. Zunge; Engl. tongue. Not from the root lih, lich, v. lingo
,
the tongue.
Lit.: fac proserpentem bestiam me duplicem ut habeam linguam (of a kiss in which the tongues touched each other),: lingua haeret metu,: in ore sita lingua est, finita dentibus,: linguā haesitantes,: linguā properanti legere,: linguā titubante loqui,: quo facilius verba ore libero exprimeret, calculos lingua volvens dicere domi solebat (Demosthenes),: linguam exserere, to thrust out the tongue, in token of derision or contempt, : so, lingua ejecta,: lingua minor,the epiglottis,.—Comically, as mock term of endearment: hujus voluptas, te opsecro, hujus mel, hujus cor, hujus labellum, hujus lingua,; cf. v. 175.—In mal. part.: homo malae linguae, a fellow with a bad tongue, i. q. fellator, ; .—
Transf.
Since the tongue is an organ of speech, a tongue, utterance, speech, language: largus opum, lingua melior,: facilem benevolumque lingua tua jam tibi me reddidit,: non tu tibi istam praetruncari linguam largiloquam jubes?: Latium beare divite linguā,: lingua quasi flabello seditionis contionem ventilare,: linguam continere,: tenere,: moderari,: linguae solutio,: linguam solvere ad jurgia,: quidam operarii linguā celeri et exercitatā,: ut vitemus linguas hominum,: Aetolorum linguas retundere,to check their tongues, bring them to silence,; cf.: claudente noxarum conscientiā linguam,: si mihi lingua foret,: ne vati noceat mala lingua futuro,: favete linguis, i. e. give attention, "be silent that you may hear," ; : linguis animisque faventes,: nam lingua mali pars pessima servi,: mercedem imponere linguae,i. e. to speak for pay,: usum linguae reciperare,: linguā debili esse,to stammer,.—Comically: os habeat, linguam, perfidiam, tongue, i. e. readiness in speech, . —
The tongue or language of a people: lingua Latina, Graeca,: Graeca et Latina lingua,: (Massilia) tam procul a Graecorum regionibus, disciplinis linguāque divisa,: quod quidem Latina lingua sic observat, ut, etc.,: Gallicae linguae scientiam habere,: qui ipsorum lingua Celtae, nostra Galli, appellantur,: dissimili linguā,: linguā utrāque,i. e. Greek and Latin,; so, auctores utriusque linguae, Quint. prooem. 1; 1, 1, 14: Mithridates, cui duas et viginti linguas notas fuisse,: haud rudis Graecae linguae,; ; : Syrus in Tiberim Orontes et linguam et mores vexit,.—
Dialect, idiom, mode of speech (post-Aug.): illis non verborum modo, sed. linguarum etiam se inter differentium copia est. : Crassus quinque Graeci sermonis differentias sic tenuit, ut, qua quisque apud eum linguā postulasset, eadem jus sibi redditum ferret,: utar enim historicā linguā,: si philosophorum linguā uti voluissem,.—
Poet. of animals. the voice, note, song, bark, etc.: linguae volucrum,; , 177: linguam praecludere (canis),.—
An utterance, expression: lingua secretior,a dark saying,.—
Of tongue-shaped things.
A plant, also called lingulaca, .—
Lingua bubula, a plant, oxtongue, bugloss, ; .—
Lingua canina, ; and lingua canis,, the plant hound's-tongue, also called cynoglossos; q. v.—
A tongue of land: id promontorium, Cujus lingua in altum proicit, Pac. ap. : lingua in altum mille passuum excurrens,; Weissenb. ad : eminet in altum lingua, in qua urbs sita est,: tenuem producit in aequora linguam,; cf.: lingua dicitur promontorii genus non excellentis sed molliter in planum devexi, Paul. ex Müll.—
A spoonful, as a measure, (al. lingulis).—
The tongue or reed of a flute, .—
The short arm of a lever: vectis lingua sub onus subdita, (cf. ligula, VII.).

la:verb:linquo.gloss: to leave, quit, forsake, depart from
senses: to leave, quit, forsake, depart from
la:verb:linquo.html:
linquo, līqui, 3 (
part. lictus, dub.), v. a.
Gr. λιπ- in λείπω, λοιπός; cf. Lat. licet
.
To leave, quit, forsake, depart from something (cf.: destituo, desero): urbem exsul linquat,: terram,: nil intentatum nostri liquere poëtae,: linquenda tellus,.—Absol., to go away: linquebat comite ancilla una,.—
Esp.
Linqui animo, and simply linqui, to swoon, faint, : linquor et ancillis excipienda cado,; so act.: me liquit animus,; .—
Linquere lumen, animam, vitam, to die: lumen linque,: dulcia linquebant labentis lumina vitae,; : linquebant dulces animas,: animam,; : nec Poenum liquere doli,. —
To leave, give up, resign, abandon something: linquamus haec,: linquamus naturam, artesque videamus,: linque severa,: spem,: inrita ventosae linquens promissa procellae,.—
To leave in any place or condition: erum in opsidione linquet,: lupos apud oves,. —
To leave behind: linquere vacuos cultoribus agros,: sui monumentum insigne pericli,: pharetram hospitio,.—
Impers. pass.: linquitur, it is left, it remains.— With ut and subj.: linquitur, ut totis animalibus adsimulentur. : et vix cernere linquitur undas, Silv. 4, 628.

la:verb:lino.html:
lĭno, lēvi (līvi), lĭtum, 3, and lĭnĭo, īvi, ītum. 4 (contr. form of the
inf. perf. lisse for livisse. : perf. livi, Cato, R. R. 69; : levi,: lini for livi, acc. to P.), v. a.
Sanscr. root li-, to let go, pour; Gr. λιβ-, λείβω; cf. Lat. libo; hence, littera, 2. limus
, to daub, besmear, anoint, to spread or rub over.
Lit.: cerā Spiramenta,: spicula vipereo felle,: carmina linenda cedro,: Sabinum quod ego ipse testa Conditum levi (sc. pice),which I have sealed with pitch,; cf. Drak. N. cr.: nam quis plura linit victuro dolia musto?: picata opercula diligenter gypso linunt,: faciem,: sucis sagittas,: cum relego, scripsisse pudet, qui plurima cerno, Me quoque, qui feci, judice digna lini, that deserve to be rubbed out, erased (because the writing on a tablet was rubbed out with the broad end of the style), .—In the form linio, īre: liquidā pice cum oleo linire,; ; : tectoria luto cum liniuntur,—
To rub over something: linere medicamenta per corpora, Ov. Med. fac. 81.—
Transf.
To overlay, cover: tecta auro, Ov. Med. fac. 7; .—
To bedaub, bemire: linit ora luto,; .—
Trop., to befoul: carmine foedo Splendida facta,.

lintĕum, i, n.

Linen: Tarquinienses (polliciti sunt) lintea in vela,.—
A sail: certum est dare lintea retro,: non tibi sunt integra lintea,: Zephyri veniant in lintea pleni,.—

senses: Any line, thread, or string, particularly
la:noun:linea.html:
līnĕa (līnĭa), ae, f.
linum
,
a linen thread, a string, line.
Lit.: nectere lineas, restes, funes,: linia longinqua per os religata,: ligato pede longā lineā gallina custoditur,: linea margaritarum triginta quinque,; cf.: lineae duae ex margaritis,; and : linea dives (of the strings of pearls which were thrown among the people at the public games), (cf. ).—
In partic.
In a net, the threads which form the meshes: licia difficile cernuntur: atque ut in plagis lineae offensae, praecipitant in sinum (of spiders' webs),.—
Transf., a net, : si feras lineis et pinna clusas contineas,.—
A fishing-line: tremulāve captum lineā trahit piscem,; .—Hence, prov.: mittere lineam, to cast a line, to fish for, try to catch a person, .—
A plumbline of masons and carpenters: perpendiculo et lineā uti,; cf.: ad regulam et lineam,; ; .—Hence,
Ad lineam and rectā lineā, in a straight line, vertically, perpendicularly: solida corpora ferri suo deorsum pondere ad lineam,; ; of the layers of stone in a wall: saxa, quae rectis lineis suos ordines servant,: (ignis) rectis lineis in caelestem locum subvolat,.—
A region, tract: linea tam rectum mundi ferit illa Leonem,that region lies directly under the lion,.—
A bowstring, Ter. Maur. praef. v. 19.—
Transf., a thread-like stroke or mark made with a pen, pencil, etc., a line: Apelli fuit perpetua consuetudo, numquam tam occupatam diem agendi, ut non, lineam ducendo, exerceret artem, quod ab eo in proverbium venit (namely, the proverb: nulla dies sine linea),: lineam cinere ducere,: candida per medium folium transcurrens,: serra in praetenui linea premente harenas (of sawing marble),: nec congruebant ad horas ejus lineae (of the sundial),; .—In geometry, a line: linea a nostris dicitur, quam γραμμὴν Graeci nominant. Eam M. Varro ita definit: Linea est, inquit, longitudo quaedam sine latitudine et altitudine,: locorum extremae lineae,: lineae, quae emittuntur ex centro,; : linea circumcurrens,a circular line, circle,.—
In partic.
A boundary-line which consisted of a narrow path between fields, ; Goes. —
In gen., a way, path: dedit sequendam calle recto lineam,.—
A barrier or line in the theatre, by which the seats were separated from each other: quid frustra refugis? cogit nos linea jungi,; : lineas poscere,.—
A feature, lineament: adulti venustissimis lineis,—
Trop.
A line of descent or kindred, lineage (post-class.): στέμματα cognationum directo limite in duas lineas separantur, quarum altera est superior, altera inferior, : clara gentis Linea,: primo gradu superioris linea continentur pater, mater,.—
An outline, sketch, design (a fig. borrowed from painting): quidam materias latius dicendo prosequebantur ... alii, cum primas modo lineas duxissent,; cf. : ea quae in Platonis oratione demiramur, non aemulari quidem, sed lineas umbrasque facere ausi sumus, .—
A boundary-line, bound, limit, end, goal: cum poëtae transilire lineas impune possint, Müll.; : si quidem est peccare tamquam transire lineas,to go beyond the mark, pass the prescribed limits,: mors ultima linea rerum est,: admoveri lineas sentio,.—Hence, prov.: amare extremā lineā, to love at a distance, i. e. to see the beloved object only at a distance, not be able to speak to her, .

,

senses: a male given name from Ancient Greek
la:other:Linus.html:
Lĭnus (-os), i, m., = Λίνος,
Linus.
A son of Apollo and Psammate, daughter of Crotopus, king of the Argives; he was given by his mother to the care of shepherds, and one day, being left alone, was torn to pieces by dogs; whereupon Apollo sent into the land a monster which destroyed everything, until slain by Chorœbus, ; sqq.—
The son of Apollo and Terpsichore, instructor of Orpheus and Hercules, the latter of whom killed him by a blow with the lyre: flam, ut ego opinor, Hercules, tu autem Linus,; ; (3, 4), 8, who confounds him with the preceding. According to others, he was a son of Mercury and Urania, and was killed by Apollo in Eubœa, ; .—
A fountain in Arcadia, .

rope, line, string, thread, cord, cable
la:noun:linum.html:
līnum, i, n.
Gr. λίνον; Goth. lein; Germ. Leinwand; Engl. linen
,
flax.
Lit.: reticulum, tenuissimo lino,: urit lini campum seges,; cf. prooem. § 2; 19, 1, 1, § 9: lino legato tam factum quam infectum continetur, quodque netum quodque in tela est,.—
Transf.
A thread, : consuto vulnere, crassum atque recens linum ostendit non una cicatrix,.—Esp., the thread with which letters were bound and legal instruments sealed: effer cito stilum, ceram et tabellas et linum,: per ceram et linum litterasque interpretes salutem mittit,: linum incidimus, legimus,.—Hence: solvere vincula epistolae,to open a letter,: lino consignare tabulas,: easque tabulas proprio lino propriaque cera consignamus,: linum ruptum,.—
A fishing line: nunc in mole sedens moderabar arundine linum,.—
A linen cloth or garment, linen: Massica Integrum perdunt lino vitiata saporem,strained through linen,; : velati lino et verbena tempora cincti,: lino vestiri aut lanis,.—
A sail: lina sinu Tendere toto, .—
A rope, cable: subducere carbasa lino,.—
A net for hunting or fishing; a hunter's net, toils: positarum lina plagarum,: nec lina sequi nodosa sinebam,; 3, 153.—A fisher's net, drag-net, ; .—Plur., : cymbae linique magister,i. e. the fisherman,; .—
A linen corselet, habergeon: fugit hasta per oras Multiplicis lini,: tempora multiplici mos est defendere lino,: thorax Multiplicis lini,.—
A string of pearls: uno lino decies sestertium inseritur,.—
A lampwick: fumigans,; : ardens,.

la:noun:linter.html:
linter, tris (nom. lintris, ), f. (m., ) [old form lunter for plun-ter; root πλύνω, to wash; cf. pluvia; hence]
Lit., a wash-tub; or in gen., a trough, vat, tray, tub, for wine, ; cf. : cavat arbore lintres,.—
Transf., a boat, skiff, wherry: lintribus materiam in insulam convehere,; : novas (sc. lintres), cavare,.—Prov.: loqui e lintre, said of one who sways his body to and fro when speaking, Julius ap. : reprehendenda et illa frequens et concitata in utramque partem nutatio, quam in Curione patre inrisit et Julius, quaerens, quis in luntre loqueretur,: naviget hinc aliā jam mihi linter aquā,i. e. let me now turn to something else,: in liquida nat tibi linter aquā,you have a favorable opportunity, (1, 5, 76).
